intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 (COQ10D2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PDSS1 gene (607429) on chromosome 10p12.1.

checks.claim: Primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 (COQ10D2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PDSS1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: PDSS1 defect has been described in three patients from two families 6, 7 carrying three pathogenic variants in the PDSS1 gene, homozygous in one family and compound heterozygote in the other (Table 1).
checks.explanation: Homozygous and compound heterozygous PDSS1 variants are described; the present family is homozygous.

checks.claim: The PDSS1 gene is located on chromosome 10p12.1.
checks.evidence_quote: A genome-wide search for homozygosity in family 1 identified a region of chromosome 10 encompassing the gene prenyldiphosphate synthase, subunit 1 (PDSS1)
checks.explanation: Chromosome 10 stated; the band 10p12.1 is standard nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 is an autosomal recessive disorder of CoQ10 biosynthesis caused by defects in PDSS1. In 1 family, quinone-dependent oxidative phosphorylation activities were reduced and were restored by adding quinone (Mollet et al., 2007). Reported patients have had sensorineural deafness followed by optic atrophy, with mild intellectual disability and muscle involvement (Nardecchia et al., 2021). One infant had a severe, progressive multisystem disorder and died at 3 years of age (Bellusci et al., 2021).

checks.claim: Primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 is an autosomal recessive disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: A genome-wide search for homozygosity in family 1 identified a region of chromosome 10
checks.explanation: Homozygosity mapping and a homozygous mutation imply recessive inheritance, but the abstract never states autosomal recessive inheritance.

checks.claim: Primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2 is a disorder of CoQ10 biosynthesis caused by defects in PDSS1.
checks.evidence_quote: We have identified 2 novel inborn errors of CoQ10 biosynthesis in 2 distinct families.
checks.explanation: PDSS1 mutation identified as cause of CoQ10 biosynthesis defect in family 1.

checks.claim: In 1 family with primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2, quinone-dependent oxidative phosphorylation activities were reduced.
checks.evidence_quote: quinone-dependent OXPHOS activities were in the range of the lowest control values, while OXPHOS enzyme activities were normal
checks.explanation: Paper says activities were in the range of the lowest control values rather than explicitly reduced.

checks.claim: In 1 family with primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency-2, reduced quinone-dependent oxidative phosphorylation activities were restored by adding quinone.
checks.evidence_quote: CoQ10 deficiency was confirmed by restoration of normal OXPHOS activities after addition of quinone.

paragraphs.text: Nardecchia et al. (2021) reported a 16-year-old girl born to consanguineous Egyptian parents. Severe language delay and profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss were diagnosed at age 4 years, and she later had mild intellectual disability. She had progressive visual loss from age 11 to 14 years, with visual acuity of 1/10 bilaterally, red-green dyschromatopsia, and optic atrophy mainly in the inferior temporal sector. Visual evoked potentials showed increased P100 latency and reduced amplitude. Optical coherence tomography showed reduced retinal nerve fiber layer thickness on both sides. She also had diffuse mild muscle weakness and mild postural tremor of the upper limbs. Brain MRI was normal. Cardiac findings were a moderately dysplastic mitral valve with moderate insufficiency, tricuspid insufficiency, and a moderately dilated left atrium.

paragraphs.text: Bellusci et al. (2021) reported a boy with primary CoQ10 deficiency. He was born prematurely after in vitro fertilization, in a pregnancy complicated by twin-twin transfusion. At 5 months of age he had failure to thrive, hypotonia, feeding difficulties, bilateral hearing impairment, pulmonary hypertension, livedo reticularis, and chronic distal phalangeal erythema. The disease progressed to a multisystem disorder with severe developmental delay, pyramidal dysfunction, seizures, tremor, optic atrophy, nystagmus, severe visual and hearing impairment, cystic white matter changes, and chronic heart failure. He died at 3 years of age. Brain MRI showed mild cerebral atrophy at 12 months. At 24 months it showed small necrotic or porencephalic cysts in the white matter around the lateral ventricles and in the commissural fibers.

paragraphs.text: Nardecchia et al. (2021) studied 2 Egyptian sisters, born to consanguineous parents, who had sensorineural deafness followed by optic atrophy. Whole-exome sequencing identified a homozygous c.735G-T transversion in the PDSS1 gene, resulting in a gln245-to-his (Q245H) substitution at a highly conserved residue (GLN245HIS). The variant lay within a 12-Mb region of homozygosity and was absent from the gnomAD database. It segregated with the disorder: both parents and an unaffected brother were heterozygous, and an unaffected sister was homozygous for the wildtype allele. Sanger sequencing of OPA1, OPA3, and WFS1 was negative.

paragraphs.text: Nardecchia et al. (2021) noted that visual system involvement in CoQ10 deficiency had been reported only in defects of the earliest steps of CoQ10 synthesis, including optic atrophy in PDSS1 deficiency. Unlike OPA1 and OPA3 defects, PDSS1 deficiency appears to cause sensorineural deafness before optic atrophy. paragraphs.text: In family 1 with CoQ10 deficiency, Mollet et al. (2007) found a homozygous nucleotide substitution in the PDSS1 gene that results in an asp308-to-glu (D308E) substitution at a conserved residue. The mutation lay in a region of homozygosity on chromosome 10. Yeast Delta-coq1 strains transformed with the corresponding mutant yeast COQ1 gene grew poorly on respiratory medium. The authors concluded that the mutation causes the OXPHOS deficiency.

paragraphs.text: In 2 Egyptian sisters, born to consanguineous parents, with sensorineural deafness followed by optic atrophy, Nardecchia et al. (2021) used whole-exome sequencing to identify a homozygous c.735G-T transversion in the PDSS1 gene. The change results in a gln245-to-his (Q245H) substitution at a highly conserved residue. The variant lay within a 12-Mb region of homozygosity and was absent from the gnomAD database. It segregated with the disorder: both parents and an unaffected brother were heterozygous, and an unaffected sister was homozygous for the wildtype allele.

paragraphs.text: Bellusci et al. (2021) reported a boy with primary CoQ10 deficiency who had a multisystem disorder and died at 3 years of age. He was compound heterozygous for 2 mutations in the PDSS1 gene (NM_014317.3). One was a c.1183C-T transition, resulting in an arg395-to-ter (R395X) substitution. The other was a c.716T-G transversion, resulting in a val239-to-gly (V239G) substitution. The patient had reduced CoQ10 levels in lymphocytes.
